chapter_theme: Against infatuation with women (மகளிர் இழிவு): their charm is like a fair-leaved poison tree, the pleasure is a dream and a whirlpool, their attachment shifts, and the sweetness at first turns bitter in the body.
structure_note: The chapter title speaks of women's baseness, but most verses describe the man's infatuation and its cost; 205 returns to other men's wives and 206 to fickle women.

204.reading: As the fruit of the etti tree cannot be eaten however good its leaves and clusters look, do not let your heart, which ought to turn away, burn for women who smile and display the beauty of their breasts.
204.nuance: The etti (strychnine tree) looks good and is poison, so the image is of an attractive surface over harm. The last line is unclear: வெய்துகொள்ளீர் may mean 'do not let it grow hot' or 'make it hard'; either way the heart is told to hold back.

205.reading: For men who enter a home seeking the wife there, the pleasure swirls them down like water in a deep pool; it seeps up like a dream and cannot be had as things are had awake.
205.nuance: Two images of the same pleasure: a whirlpool that drags one under, and a dream that leaves nothing. The grammar of the first two lines is loose, and I am not sure whether the whirling water is the pleasure or the woman.

206.reading: Women graceful as young she-elephants, though they cling like grass under a storm and say even the gods would be bewitched and bid a man stay near, turn to talk with strangers and are gone.
206.nuance: The middle lines are hard to construe; I take மயலுறும் வானவர் as the women's boast that even gods are enchanted by them. The point that survives any construal is the turn to others (அயலுறப் பேசி) and the leaving.

207.reading: Joining with young women in this world, the lot set for the body, is sweet cane juice from the press in the hand and turns to bitter neem within the body.
207.nuance: The contrast is in the place: sweet in the hand (கையகத்தே), bitter in the body (மெய்யகத்தே). The second line, மெய்யகத்தோடும் வைத்த விதியது, may mean that this is the fate attached to having a body; I am not sure of it.

208.reading: Weak-willed conduct is like wading to the middle of a moss-covered pond to sound its depth; unless such men are tied down and held back, they go the way of those who crawl into a narrow hole.
208.nuance: The moss-covered pond hides its depth, an image of danger under a smooth surface. பூழை is a narrow opening; it may be a plain trap image or a euphemism for the woman's body. The verse is obscure and my construal is tentative.

links.note: Both say a woman's attractive surface hides what should repel: the Naladiyar the body's foulness under the skin, Tirumular poison under fair leaves and fruit.
Both shrink the adulterer's pleasure: small against great fear in the Naladiyar, a dream and a whirlpool in Tirumular.
Both describe a woman who promises closeness and then turns away; the Naladiyar's said she would never part, Tirumular's bids the man stay near and leaves talking to others.

Both use sugarcane to show sweetness changing over time: the Naladiyar's cane eaten from the tip grows sweeter like the friendship of the learned, Tirumular's cane juice in the hand turns to neem in the body.

205 says the pleasure of the man who enters another's home seeps up like a dream and cannot be had as things are had awake (கனவது போலக் ... நனவது போலவும் நாடவொண்ணாதே). In Kural 1215 the woman sets waking and dream side by side and finds each sweet when seen (நனவினால் கண்டதூஉம் ... கனவுந்தான்). The same dream and waking pair, which the Kural uses to make the dream equal to waking, 205 uses to show the stolen pleasure is no more than a dream.

208 likens weak-willed conduct to wading to the middle of a moss-covered pond to sound its depth (குளமூடு பாசியில் ஆழ நடுவர்). 1506 says the mind of those who only recite and gather flowers is a stone dropped in a mossy pond (பாசிக் குளத்தில்வீழ் கல்). Tirumular uses the moss-covered pond twice for a mind that sinks out of sight, once in lust and once in empty ritual.
